title: He Clipped the Last Hurdle and Still Broke the National Record. Tejas Shirse Is Going to Glasgow.
excerpt: The 24-year-old hurdler ran 13.27 seconds in Ludhiana on Friday, shattering his own 110m hurdles record and becoming the first Indian male hurdler to qualify for the Commonwealth Games since 2014.
body:
Last month at the Federation Cup in Ranchi, Tejas Shirse won gold in the 110m hurdles with a time of 13.50 seconds. It was not fast enough. The Athletics Federation of India had set a Commonwealth Games qualification standard of 13.39 seconds, and Shirse was eleven hundredths of a second on the wrong side of it.

Then the AFI did something unusual. It announced the Indian Athletics Series 9 in Ludhiana as a last-chance qualification event. For Shirse, it was an unexpected reprieve.

On Friday at Guru Nanak Stadium, the 24-year-old delivered the run of his life.

Shirse clocked **13.27 seconds** in the B final, breaking his own national record of 13.41 seconds — a mark that had stood since 2024 — by a full 0.14 seconds. He clipped the final hurdle but never lost momentum, crossing the line well clear of Krishik M, who finished second in 13.55 seconds.

"That celebration came from deep within," Shirse told The Indian Express after the race. "I had no expectations for today. This event wasn't even part of my plans. I simply enjoyed the experience."

## A 12-Year Drought Ends

If selected for the Indian squad, Shirse will become the first Indian male hurdler to compete at the Commonwealth Games since Siddharth Thingalaya represented the country in Glasgow in 2014. That is a 12-year gap in one of track and field's most technically demanding sprint events.

The timing of Shirse's breakthrough is significant. He had spent four months away from competition due to injury earlier this year, and the Federation Cup in Ranchi was supposed to be his final shot at qualification. The additional meet in Ludhiana was not on his calendar.

"I always believed it was within my reach," Shirse said. "My performances were promising, yet I couldn't better my time until now. Upon my return from injury, I assured everyone that breaking the national record was possible."

## India Joins an Elite Asian Club

Shirse's 13.27-second effort currently ranks sixth-fastest in Asia this season, behind Japan's Rachid Muratake (13.05s), Shunsuke Izumiya (13.13s), China's Junxi Liu (13.22s), Yuanjiang Chen (13.22s), and Japan's Tatsuki Abe (13.26s).

The performance makes India only the third Asian nation — after Japan and China — to produce a sub-13.30-second athlete in the men's 110m hurdles. For a country that has traditionally focused its sprint resources on the 100m and 200m flat events, the milestone marks a shift in competitive depth.

Shirse, who represents the Reliance Foundation, has been steadily climbing since first breaking the national record in 2024. His progression from 13.41 to 13.27 represents the kind of incremental-then-sudden improvement that Indian athletics has long needed in the technical events.

## The Road to Glasgow

The 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow are scheduled for July, leaving Shirse roughly a month to prepare. Elsewhere at the Ludhiana meet, javelin throwers Rohit Yadav (83.76m) and Yashvir Singh (82.93m) also cleared their CWG qualification marks, while World Championships finalist Sachin Yadav notably skipped the event — his best throw this season of 81.95m remains below the 82.61m standard.

For NRIs in the UK, Glasgow offers a rare chance to watch Indian athletes compete on home soil. Shirse's event, the 110m hurdles, is one of the most spectacular in track and field — ten barriers in roughly 13 seconds, with margins measured in hundredths.

## What It Means for Indian Sprinting

India's track and field programme has historically produced its best results in throws and middle-distance events. Neeraj Chopra's Olympic gold in the javelin, Avinash Sable's steeplechase exploits, and the women's 4x400m relay team's consistent performances all came from outside the sprint disciplines. The hurdles, in particular, have been a blindspot — the event demands not just raw speed but also technical precision over ten barriers, and India has struggled to produce specialists who can compete at the continental level.

Shirse's sub-13.30 run signals a shift. At 24, he has at least two more Olympic cycles ahead of him. The 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and the 2036 Games — which India is bidding to host — both sit within his competitive window. If he can continue shaving hundredths off his time, he could become India's first genuinely competitive Olympic hurdler.

On Friday in Ludhiana, those hundredths finally fell on the right side.

*Sources: The Indian Express, PTI, Yardbarker, Dainik News Live*
